title: Iterators and generators: lazy pipelines
summary: The iterator protocol, one-shot iterators, generator functions and their states, `yield from`, lazy pipelines with itertools, and the mutate-while-iterating trap.
prerequisiteNotes: Functions, closures and the itertools recap from py-functions-closures. Generator expressions from py-sequences-unpacking are assumed.
objectives: Explain the iterator protocol and the difference between an iterable and an iterator, including one-shot exhaustion.
Write generator functions with `yield` and `yield from`, and name a generator's states from creation to close.
Compose lazy pipelines from generators and `itertools`, bound infinite sources, and materialise only at the edge.
Spot mutation-during-iteration bugs and choose the right fix.

concepts.title: The iterator protocol
concepts.body: An **iterable** is anything `iter()` accepts. `iter(obj)` returns an **iterator**: an object whose `__next__` hands out one item per call and raises `StopIteration` when it has nothing left. Iterators also define `__iter__` returning themselves, so they work in `for` too. `for`, `list()`, `sum()`, `max()`, unpacking and `in` all drive this same protocol. `next(it, default)` returns the default instead of raising.
concepts.code:
xs = [10, 20]
it = iter(xs)             # calls xs.__iter__()
print(next(it))           # 10
print(next(it))           # 20
print(next(it, 'done'))   # 'done' instead of StopIteration

# what `for x in xs: print(x)` really does
it = iter(xs)
while True:
    try:
        x = next(it)
    except StopIteration:
        break
    print(x)

concepts.title: Iterable versus iterator: one pass only
concepts.body: Containers such as `list`, `dict`, `str` and `range` are re-iterable: every `iter()` call returns a fresh iterator. Generators, `map`, `filter`, `zip`, `enumerate`, file objects and every `itertools` result **are** iterators: one pass, then empty, with no error on the second pass. That silence is the bug. A function that loops over its argument twice works with a list and quietly returns a wrong answer for a generator. Materialise once with `list(it)`, or require a re-iterable argument. `x in it` on an iterator also consumes items up to the match.
concepts.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
print(iter(nums) is iter(nums))   # False: fresh iterator each time
it = iter(nums)
print(iter(it) is it)             # True: an iterator is its own iterator
print(sum(it), sum(it))           # 6 0

squares = (n * n for n in nums)
print(4 in squares, list(squares))  # True [9]: 1 and 4 were consumed

concepts.title: Generator functions and their four states
concepts.body: Any function containing `yield` is a generator function. Calling it runs **none** of the body; it returns a generator object in state `GEN_CREATED`. Each `next()` runs the body (`GEN_RUNNING`) up to the next `yield`, which hands out a value and freezes the frame with all its locals (`GEN_SUSPENDED`). A `return` or falling off the end raises `StopIteration`, carrying any returned value as `.value`, and the generator is `GEN_CLOSED` for good. `g.close()` raises `GeneratorExit` at the paused `yield`, so `finally` blocks and `with` exits still run.
concepts.code:
import inspect

def countdown(n):
    print('started')
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
    return 'liftoff'                  # becomes StopIteration.value

g = countdown(2)
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))  # GEN_CREATED, nothing printed yet
print(next(g))                       # started, then 2
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))  # GEN_SUSPENDED
print(next(g))                       # 1
try:
    next(g)
except StopIteration as stop:
    print(stop.value)                # liftoff
print(inspect.getgeneratorstate(g))  # GEN_CLOSED

concepts.title: yield from, and send in one paragraph
concepts.body: `yield from sub` re-yields everything `sub` produces and then evaluates to the sub-generator's return value. It is the clean way to write recursive generators such as tree walks and flattening. `g.send(v)` resumes a paused generator and makes the paused `yield` expression evaluate to `v`; plain `next(g)` is `send(None)`. A fresh generator must be primed with `next(g)` first, because sending a non-None value to a just-started generator raises `TypeError`. Know `send` exists for coroutine-style code; interview solutions rarely need it.

concepts.title: Lazy pipelines keep memory flat
concepts.body: Chain generators and each item travels the whole pipeline before the next one is read. The consumer **pulls**; every stage holds about one item, so memory is O(1) whatever the input size, and the same code works on unbounded input such as a log tail or a socket. Eager lists keep every intermediate result alive. Some steps cannot stay lazy: `sorted()` and `list()` materialise everything, and `len()` and `reversed()` do not accept a generator at all. Put such steps last, or replace them (a size-k heap instead of a full sort for top-k).

concepts.title: itertools for lazy work
concepts.body: `islice(it, stop)` or `islice(it, start, stop, step)` slices any iterator lazily (no negative indices). `count`, `cycle` and `repeat` are infinite, so bound them with `islice`, `zip` or `takewhile`. `pairwise` yields overlapping neighbour pairs; `chain` and `chain.from_iterable` concatenate. `tee(it, n)` gives n independent iterators, but it buffers every item one copy has seen and another has not, so if one copy runs far ahead it costs as much as a list, and the original iterator must not be touched afterwards. `accumulate`, `groupby` (consecutive keys only) and `product`/`permutations`/`combinations` are recapped in py-functions-closures. They are lazy too, which matters: `permutations(range(10))` has 3,628,800 tuples.
concepts.code:
from itertools import islice, count, cycle, chain, pairwise, tee, takewhile

print(list(islice(count(10, 5), 3)))                   # [10, 15, 20]
print(list(islice(cycle('ab'), 5)))                    # ['a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a']
print(list(pairwise([1, 4, 9])))                       # [(1, 4), (4, 9)]
print(list(takewhile(lambda n: n < 20, count(1, 7))))  # [1, 8, 15]
print(list(chain.from_iterable([[1], [], [2, 3]])))    # [1, 2, 3]
a, b = tee(iter([1, 2, 3]))
print(list(a), list(b))                                # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]

concepts.title: Never resize what you are iterating
concepts.body: A list iterator walks by index. Removing an item mid-loop shifts the rest left, so the item after it is skipped; appending can make the loop run forever. Dicts and sets detect a size change and raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (assigning to existing keys is fine). The fixes: build a new collection with a comprehension, or loop over a snapshot (`list(d)`, `xs[:]`) and mutate the original.

task: Write `first_jumps(lines, threshold, limit)`. `lines` is a list of strings from a sensor log. Strip each line, then ignore blank lines, lines starting with `#`, and lines that are not integers. For each pair of consecutive valid readings compute `later - earlier`, keep the differences whose absolute value is at least `threshold`, and return the first `limit` of them as a list. Build it as a lazy pipeline so no work is done past the `limit`-th jump.
starter:
from itertools import islice, pairwise

def first_jumps(lines, threshold, limit):
    # 1. a generator function that yields the valid int readings
    # 2. pairwise -> differences -> keep the big ones
    # 3. return list(islice(..., limit))
    return []
hints: Put the parsing in its own generator function: `continue` on blanks and comments, wrap only `int(line)` in `try`/`except ValueError`, then `yield` the value. `int()` already accepts a sign and surrounding spaces.

`pairwise(readings)` gives `(earlier, later)` neighbours. A generator expression computes the difference, a second one filters by `abs(d) >= threshold`, and `list(islice(jumps, limit))` caps and materialises.
checklist: Parsing lives in a generator function, not a list built up front.
I use `pairwise` and `islice` instead of index arithmetic.
I materialise with `list()` once, at the very end.
pitfalls: Looping over an iterator argument twice: the second pass is silently empty.
Expecting a generator function's body (its prints, validation or side effects) to run when it is called rather than on the first `next()`.
Removing from a list while looping over it, or resizing a dict or set mid-loop.
Calling `list()`, `sum()` or `sorted()` on an infinite iterator such as `count()` or `cycle()`.
Using `tee` and then letting one copy run far ahead, or still using the original iterator.
Raising `StopIteration` by hand to end a generator; use `return`, because a StopIteration escaping a generator body is turned into `RuntimeError`.

walkthrough.title: Pull, don't push: tracing the pipeline
walkthrough.body: Building `readings`, `deltas` and `jumps` runs nothing; it only wires generators together. `list(islice(jumps, limit))` asks islice for an item, islice asks the filter, the filter asks the difference expression, that asks `pairwise`, and `pairwise` asks the parser, which reads lines until one parses. Once islice has handed out `limit` items it stops asking, so the rest of the log is never read.

walkthrough.title: Solve the task in three moves
walkthrough.body: First, isolate the messy part in a generator function: strip, skip blanks and comments, `continue` on `ValueError`. Second, compose: `pairwise` for neighbours, one generator expression for the difference and one for the threshold. Third, cap and materialise at the edge with `list(islice(..., limit))`. Then say the complexity out loud: O(n) time worst case, O(1) memory besides the output, and early exit once `limit` jumps are found.

extraPractice.title: Repeat to length
extraPractice.prompt: Write `take_cycle(items, n)` that returns the first `n` items of `items` repeated end to end. Return [] when `items` is empty or `n` is 0.
hints: `itertools.cycle(items)` repeats forever, so never call `list()` on it directly.
`islice(cycle(items), n)` stops after n. Cycling an empty list is simply empty, so no special case is needed.
checklist: I bound the infinite iterator with `islice`.
An empty list or n = 0 gives [].

extraPractice.title: Fair interleave
extraPractice.prompt: Write `interleave(lists)` that takes one item from each list in turn, skipping lists that have run out, until every list is exhausted. Items can be any value, including None and False.
hints: Keep a `deque` of iterators, one `iter(xs)` per list. Pop one from the left, take its next item, and put it back on the right only if it produced one.
`next(it, sentinel)` with `sentinel = object()` tells 'exhausted' apart from a real None item without try/except.
checklist: Uneven lengths keep going after the short lists run out.
A None or False item is not mistaken for 'exhausted'.
Each list is walked once through its iterator; nothing is indexed.

followUps.question: How do you make your own class iterable, and can it be iterated twice?
followUps.answer: Write `__iter__` as a generator method, for example `def __iter__(self): yield from self._items`. Every `for` calls `__iter__` again and gets a fresh generator, so the object is re-iterable and nested loops over it work. Avoid making the container its own iterator (`__iter__` returning self plus `__next__`): that makes it one-shot.

followUps.question: Your generator validates its arguments, but the error shows up far from the call. Why, and how do you fix it?
followUps.answer: A generator function's body does not run until the first `next()`, so a `raise ValueError` at its top fires wherever the generator is first consumed. Split it: an ordinary function validates eagerly, then returns an inner generator or a generator expression.

followUps.question: What happens if a `StopIteration` escapes from inside a generator body?
followUps.answer: It would look exactly like normal exhaustion and silently truncate the output, so Python converts it into a `RuntimeError`. The usual trigger is a bare `next(it)` on an empty iterator inside a generator. Use `next(it, default)` or catch it, and end a generator with `return`.

followUps.question: When would you not use a generator?
followUps.answer: When you need `len`, indexing or several passes, when the data is small and a list is clearer to print and debug, or when the next step must see everything anyway: laziness in front of a full sort saves little.

takeaways: `for` calls `iter()` once and `next()` until `StopIteration`; everything iterable plugs into that protocol.
Containers are re-iterable; generators, map, zip and file objects are one-shot and go silently empty.
Calling a generator function runs nothing; each `next()` resumes it to the next `yield`.
Lazy pipelines hold about one item per stage: bound infinite sources with `islice` and call `list()` only at the edge.
Never resize a list, dict or set while iterating it: build a new one or loop over a snapshot.

diagrams.title: What a for loop does
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram. The for loop calls iter on the list and receives a list iterator. It then calls next on the iterator repeatedly, receiving 10 and then 20. The third next call raises StopIteration, which the loop catches and treats as the end.
diagrams.caption: One iter() call, then next() until StopIteration. The loop swallows StopIteration; you never see it.

messages.label: iter(xs)
messages.note: Called once, before the first pass of the body.

messages.label: new iterator
messages.note: A list hands out a fresh iterator every time, so it can be looped again.

messages.label: raise StopIteration
messages.note: The loop catches it and ends normally. The iterator is now exhausted for good.

diagrams.title: One generator, two consumers
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. On the left a single generator of squares feeds sum, which gets 14, and then list, which gets an empty list. On the right the squares are materialised into a list once, and both sum and max read it correctly.
diagrams.caption: An iterator is drained by its first consumer. If you need two passes, materialise once.

before.label: Share a generator: second pass empty

diagrams.title: A generator's life
diagrams.alt: State diagram of a generator. It starts in GEN_CREATED. next() moves it to GEN_RUNNING. A yield moves it to GEN_SUSPENDED, where it waits for the caller, whose next() or send() resumes it into GEN_RUNNING. A return or exception from running, or close() while suspended, moves it to GEN_CLOSED.
diagrams.caption: Only next(), send(), throw() or close() move a generator. Between calls it is frozen at a yield, locals intact.

steps.text: Calling `gen()` runs no code. The first `next()` starts the body from the top.
`yield` hands a value to the caller and freezes the frame: locals, loop position and `try` blocks are all kept.
`next()` resumes right after the `yield`; `send(v)` does the same and makes the `yield` expression evaluate to v.
`return` or falling off the end raises `StopIteration` for the caller. An exception propagates out. Either way the generator is closed.
`close()` raises `GeneratorExit` at the paused `yield`, so `finally` and `with` cleanup still run. Further `next()` calls just raise `StopIteration`.

diagrams.title: The first_jumps pipeline
diagrams.alt: Data-flow diagram left to right: input lines feed parse_readings, which feeds pairwise, which feeds a filter of large differences, which feeds islice with the limit. Below islice, list() collects the result. The consumer pulls items from the end of the chain.
diagrams.caption: Each item flows end to end before the next line is read. islice stops pulling at the limit, so later lines are never touched.

steps.text: `list()` asks islice for an item. Nothing upstream has run yet.
The request travels back to the parser, which reads lines until one parses as an int. `pairwise` needs two readings before it can emit its first pair.
Each pair becomes a difference; small ones are dropped and the filter asks for the next pair.
After `limit` jumps islice stops asking, and the remaining lines are never read or parsed.

diagrams.title: Items held at peak, 1,000 input lines
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of items held in memory at peak for a three-stage pipeline over 1,000 lines where every item survives. Three stored list stages hold 3,000 items, generators followed by sorted hold 1,000, and three generator stages hold about 3.
diagrams.caption: Counts follow from the code, assuming every item survives each stage and each eager list stays bound to a name. A sort forces the whole input into memory.

diagrams.title: Removing while looping
diagrams.alt: Side-by-side comparison. On the left a for loop removes 2 from the list 1, 2, 2, 3 while iterating it, so the index moves past the second 2 and the result is 1, 2, 3. On the right a comprehension reads the original list and builds a new list 1, 3.
diagrams.caption: The list iterator tracks an index, not an item. Build a new list instead of shrinking the one you are walking.

exercises.starter:
from itertools import islice, pairwise

def first_jumps(lines, threshold, limit):
    # 1. a generator function that yields the valid int readings
    # 2. pairwise -> differences -> keep the big ones
    # 3. return list(islice(..., limit))
    return []

def interleave(lists):
    return [x for group in zip(*lists) for x in group]

predict.code:
def gen():
    print('start')
    yield 1

g = gen()
print('made')
print(next(g))
predict.explain: Calling `gen()` only creates the generator; the body, including its print, runs on the first `next()`.
Both arguments are the same iterator, so each tuple takes two consecutive items. zip stops when it cannot fill a tuple, so 5 is dropped.

predict.code:
def inner():
    yield 1
    return 'done'

def outer():
    result = yield from inner()
    yield result

print(list(outer()))
predict.explain: `yield from` re-yields 1, then evaluates to inner's return value. outer yields that as a normal item.
Index 0 removes the first 2 and the list becomes [2, 3, 2]; index 1 is 3; index 2 is the last 2, and `remove` deletes the first 2, leaving [3, 2]. The loop then runs past the end.

predict.code:
def acc():
    total = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total
        total += x

g = acc()
next(g)
g.send(5)
print(g.send(10))
predict.explain: `next(g)` primes it at the first yield. `send(5)` makes x = 5 and total 5; `send(10)` makes total 15, which the next yield hands back.
`map` returns a one-shot iterator. The first `list()` drains it and the second finds nothing, with no error.

lab.tip: When you reach for a generator, say why out loud: 'this keeps memory at O(1) and stops reading once we have k results.' Then name the cost: it is one-shot, so if anything needs two passes, materialise once with list().
